unit.title: What agents are, and when to trust them

lesson.title: When to trust an agent
lesson.subtitle: Check what it did, and match trust to the stakes

video.title: When to trust an agent
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)

chapters.label: A reminder for a lesson that doesn’t exist
Trust and stakes, and the lab

scenes.visual: A list: “No school”; It carried on.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Our agent set a colleague a reminder for Saturday, for a lesson that doesn’t exist! There’s no school on Saturday. The timetable even said so. It just carried on.

scenes.animation: The Darsi mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: when to trust an agent, and how to check it.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Sure is not the same as right
scenes.narration: An agent sounds just as sure when it’s wrong. Darsi Tiny picks the right tool and every detail about ninety-seven times in a hundred, with wordings it learned. With new wordings, it’s closer to four in five. And it never says, I’m not sure.

scenes.visual: A list: Copies a name wrongly; Misreads a new wording; Carries on after a failure.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Three slips come up again and again. It copies a name wrongly: class 9Z became 9C. It misreads a new way of asking. And it carries on after a step fails, like that Saturday reminder.

scenes.visual: A list: Which tool did it call?; With which details?; What came back?; Does the answer match it?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: So don’t judge an agent by how its answer sounds. Check what it did. Which tool did it call, with which details? What did the tool give back, and does the answer match it?

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Let’s check that Saturday reminder. The first call asked the timetable for 6B on Saturday. The result came back: no school. Then it set a reminder that just says 6B: 6B. The slip was there to see, in the result.

scenes.visual: A list: Fetch books: fine; The register: check it; Letters home: read first.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Think of a new teaching assistant. You’d let them fetch books on day one. You’d check their register for weeks. And you’d read any letter home before it goes.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The agent’s answer sounds right. What should you check, to know it really is?

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Check the call and the result
scenes.narration: The call and the result. A confident sentence tells you nothing. The call shows what it asked for, and the result shows what came back. If the answer doesn’t match the result, don’t use it.

scenes.visual: A list: Looking up: a quick check; Actions: you approve first; About a child: a person decides.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Match your trust to the stakes. Looking up the weather or a library book: a quick check is enough. Reminders and messages: you approve them first. Marks, attendance or anything about a child: a person decides, every time.

scenes.visual: A list: Four claims about the Nile; Correct, wrong, or a source?; One is invented.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: check the AI’s answer
scenes.narration: In the app, an AI answer about the Nile has four claims. Mark each one: correct, wrong, or check a source. One is invented, yet sounds just as sure.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Which of these should an agent never do on its own: look up tomorrow’s weather, find a library book, or change a pupil’s mark?

scenes.visual: Summary points: Sure is not proof; Check the call and the result; Trust to match the stakes.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Sure is not proof · Check the call and the result · Trust to match the stakes
scenes.narration: Changing a mark: a person decides that. Remember: sounding sure is not proof. Check the call, the details and the result. And match your trust to the stakes.

scenes.visual: A list: Three agent conversations; Find the hidden slip; Green, amber or red?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: play Spot the slip. Write three short agent conversations on the board, each with a call, a result and an answer. Hide a slip in two of them. Pupils find each slip, and rate each job green, amber or red.

checkpoints.prompt: An agent’s answer sounds right. What should you check, to know it really is?

options.text: The tool it called, its details and the result

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the call shows what it asked for and the result shows what came back. The answer must match them.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a confident or fast answer proves nothing. Check the call and the result, and whether the answer matches them.

checkpoints.prompt: Which of these should an agent never do on its own?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a mark is a decision about a child, so a person makes it. Looking things up only needs a quick check.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — looking things up is low risk. Changing a pupil’s mark is a decision about a child: a person makes it.
